source.title: Training Trajectories of Language Models Across Scales
source.authors: Mengzhou Xia; Mikel Artetxe; Chunting Zhou; Xi Victoria Lin; Ramakanth Pasunuru; Danqi Chen; Luke Zettlemoyer; Ves Stoyanov

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present, including appendices; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: It measures held-out validation perplexity across model-training trajectories and relates downstream task performance to perplexity, but it does not fit or evaluate the original scaling-law prediction method.
record.gate_note: The paper reports validation-perplexity trajectories for six OPT sizes against training FLOPs and describes them as following a similar power-law pattern. It does not fit exponents, predict larger runs from smaller runs, or test compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. Perplexities of generated or corrupted text are not held-out pretraining-loss results for these versions and are omitted.
record.test_reason: The study analyses intermediate checkpoints of six OPT sizes (125M–175B). It reports held-out validation perplexity against training FLOPs (Fig. 1) and 2-shot BIG-Bench accuracy against validation perplexity, FLOPs, tokens and steps (Fig. 8, 9, 17, 18). That bears on V6 directly and on V1 only qualitatively. No exponents are fitted and no extrapolation or allocation is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that validation perplexity predicts OPT model behaviour better than model size or training compute, including downstream 2-shot ICL accuracy across sizes. Larger models also unlock new phenomena as perplexity falls further. They note exceptions: on texts generated by contrasting two models, models at the same perplexity behave differently, so their distributions are not identical.
record.recipe_differences: Analyzes intermediate OPT checkpoints and behavior trajectories rather than fitting scaling-law exponents or testing predictions from small-run fits.
record.method_sensitivity: Downstream task ordering changes with the matched training budget: equal FLOPs versus equal training tokens or steps.

fits_no_version.finding: On randomly corrupted text (20–100% random tokens) and on incorrect multiple-choice options, perplexity falls as model size grows (Fig. 5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scaling lowers perplexity even on out-of-distribution or noisy text.

fits_no_version.finding: Text decoded from ps−pl (125M minus 30B) shows inverse scaling: perplexity rises with model size across all OPT sizes and in GPT-Neo (Fig. 6, 7).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some text distributions show inverse loss scaling with model size.

fits_no_version.finding: A subset of tokens shows double-descent perplexity trajectories in larger models at similar validation perplexity (Fig. 4, 12).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Token-level loss is non-monotone even when aggregate loss falls smoothly.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The loss scaling evidence is presented as a plot with no tabulated values, fitted exponents, or quantified power-law range. The study focuses on OPT models trained with the same data and similar procedures. Downstream results cover only 2-shot multiple-choice tasks, and the authors note that task aggregation may conceal individual-task patterns.

untested.parts: No separate loss-vs-parameters or loss-vs-tokens fits, no exponents, no quantified range. Only within-run trajectories vs FLOPs are shown.
No compute-optimal allocation analysis. The equal-FLOPs comparison uses intermediate checkpoints, not tuned runs per budget.
No shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
Text only. OPT uses repeated data (300B tokens, 180B unique) but repetition is not varied.
Only 2-shot multiple-choice BIG-Bench tasks, in a single model family with the same data.
No comparison of fitting or setup choices.

missing.what: Linearity (12) vs breakthroughness (6) task groups. Breakthrough-task accuracy rises sharply once validation PPL drops below about 8, while linearity tasks rise gradually.
Per-task trajectories have high variance. Breakthrough tasks grow smoothly along the trajectory, but the authors say per-task prediction remains challenging.

record.verdict_notes: R1–R6 rest on a single qualitative sentence about within-run trajectories under an LR schedule. They are weak evidence for V1, and treating them as six independent rows overstates it. The equal-FLOPs result (R13) compares intermediate checkpoints and should not be read as evidence on V3. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No separate loss-versus-parameter or loss-versus-token fit; no fitted exponents or quantified range of power-law validity. The reported trajectory is validation perplexity versus training FLOPs.
No small-run fit is used to predict loss on larger runs.
No fixed-compute sweep identifies loss-minimising parameter and token allocations.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No tests across other modalities or training regimes. OPT training uses repeated data, but there is no comparison testing the law under repetition.
Downstream evaluation is limited to 2-shot multiple-choice tasks from BIG-Bench; generation-based tasks and other downstream settings are not tested.
No comparison of fitting choices, parameter-counting conventions, or alternative scaling-law fits.

source_check.notes: The authors' conclusion is accurately paraphrased. V1 evidence is qualitative perplexity scaling; V6 evidence concerns a common OPT training setup and selected multiple-choice tasks, without calibrated out-of-scale accuracy forecasts.

statements.correction: OPT: limits_scope for parameter-based ordering across budget axes; smaller models outperform at matched FLOPs except 125M; larger models outperform at matched tokens or steps; accuracy aligns across sizes at matched validation perplexity (Section 5.2, Figure 8).
statements.problem: The OPT ordering is correct, but challenges overstates its implication for V6: the budget dependence qualifies parameter-based prediction while validation perplexity remains predictive.
